newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry cheers move to privatise airports.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry cheers move to privatise airports.

text.p: A leading Indian industry organisation on Thursday cheered the government's decision to privatise management and facilities at national airports and frame a comprehensive civil aviation policy within two months.

"The policy will bring about transparency and definiteness on issues such as opening up the skies and foreign investment," H.L. Somany, president of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM) said in a statement.
On Wednesday, Jayanti Natarajan, a junior civil aviation minister, said her ministry was drafting a policy whereby a large part of airport management would be privatised.
She said the concept of greenfield airports, joint sector ventures between state and federal governments was also under consideration.
Natarajan said the government would continue to control only air space management and runways, and stressed the need to open up larger air corridors and improve maintenance of aircraft.

ASSOCHAM's Somany said the absence of a clear policy had led to a lot of confusion. "In case of Tata-Singapore Airlines proposal, the foreign investment promotion board cleared it ... the government deferred the decision ... and referred the issue back to the Civil Aviation Ministry," he said.
In April, the centre-left United Front government barred foreign airlines from holding any equity stakes in the domestic aviation sector.
The decision scuttled a proposed $600-million tie-up between Singapore Airlines Ltd and India's Tata group.

It also forced Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways to start finding ways to offload their 20 percent stakes in private carrier Jet Airways. The government gave the foreign partners of Jet Airways until October 15 to sell their stakes.
Nearly a dozen private airlines sprang up after the government ended its monopoly as part of an economic liberalisation programme that began in 1991.

But most private airlines, weighed down by crippling fuel costs, low passenger fares and government laws that force them to fly to remote, unprofitable regions, are foundering. Only three private airlines are currently flying.
